extracted.intended_audience: immigration officers, consular officers, immigration attorneys, policy stakeholders, and members of the public submitting comments
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and legal standards for determining whether a noncitizen is likely to become a public charge for visa, admission, adjustment of status, extension of stay, or change of status purposes under INA section 212(a)(4). Includes definitions, exempt benefits, required factors, evidentiary processes, and mitigation (e.g., bonds, affidavits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Benefits Exempt under PRWORA
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress excluded certain benefits (available to all aliens regardless of qualified status) from the federal public benefit definition under PRWORA (8 U.S.C. 1611(b)). Examples listed include emergency medical assistance (8 U.S.C. 1611(b)(1)(A)), short-term non-cash in-kind emergency disaster relief, public health assistance for immunizations, payments for foster care and adoption, student assistance under the Higher Education Act, means-tested programs under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, Head Start benefits, benefits under title I of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, and Food Stamps for children under 18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are benefits Congress made available to all aliens; DHS notes these benefits would not be part of the public charge determination under the proposed rule (see 8 U.S.C. 1611(b)). Citations: 8 U.S.C. 1611(b); examples and clarifying agency guidance are provided in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical assistance for emergency medical condition (PRWORA exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical assistance under title XIX of the Social Security Act for care and services necessary for the treatment of an emergency medical condition (as defined in section 1903(v)(3)), not related to an organ transplant procedure, if the alien otherwise meets the State plan eligibility requirements (other than certain income/aid requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific category is described as an exemption in 8 U.S.C. 1611(b) and is treated separately from other title XIX benefits; eligibility still depends on meeting State plan requirements aside from some specified exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term, non-cash, in-kind emergency disaster relief (PRWORA exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term, non-cash, in-kind emergency disaster relief is an exempt category under PRWORA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include FEMA and related disaster programs such as D-SNAP; described as relief provided by FEMA and other agencies to low-income households with disaster-related losses. See DHS preamble citations and DisasterAssistance.gov examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test for community programs necessary for protection of life or safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Justice (Final Specification of Community Programs Necessary for Protection of Life or Safety) provided a three-part test to identify excluded community-based programs: (1) the programs deliver in-kind (non-cash) services at the community level (including through public or private nonprofit agencies), do not condition provision/amount/cost on individual income or resources, and serve protection-of-life-or-safety purposes; (2) the programs are limited to in-kind benefits and are open without regard to income or resources (programs that condition assistance on income/resources are excluded); and (3) included programs are those necessary for the protection of life or safety (examples listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs must satisfy all three prongs to be excluded. The preamble reproduces the test and then lists types of included programs (e.g., crisis counseling, short-term shelter, heat/cold assistance, soup kitchens, medical/public health services, activities designed to protect life/safety). Citation: Final Specification of Community Programs Necessary for Protection of Life or Safety Under Welfare Reform Legislation, 66 FR 3613 (Jan. 16, 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of community programs considered necessary for protection of life or safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Included program types (as examples of programs that meet the three-part test): crisis counseling and intervention; child protection and adult protective services; violence and abuse prevention and victims services; treatment of mental illness or substance abuse; short-term shelter or housing assistance for homeless or victims of domestic violence; programs to help individuals during adverse weather; soup kitchens, community food banks, senior nutrition programs; medical and public health services (including treatment and prevention) and mental health/disability/substance abuse assistance necessary to protect life or safety; activities designed to protect the life or safety of workers, children, youths, or community residents; and any other necessary programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is illustrative and tied to the three-part test; programs meeting the three-prong criteria are excluded from 'federal public benefit' considerations under PRWORA.

rubrics_metrics.name: INS definition of 'public charge' (1999 Interim Field Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: INS defined 'public charge' to mean 'the likelihood of a foreign national becoming primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either: (1) Receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance; or (2) Institutionalization for long-term care at government expense.' Former INS defined 'primarily dependent' as 'the majority' or 'more than 50 percent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1999 guidance formed the basis for INS's approach: primary dependence shown by cash assistance or government-funded long-term institutionalization. INS consulted agencies (HHS, SSA, USDA) in developing this interpretation; some agencies advised that receipt of certain benefits (e.g., SSI) could show primary dependence, while others (USDA re: food stamps) advised certain nutrition programs should not be considered. DHS notes these interagency views may not remain fully relevant given shifts in proposed definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: IIRIRA minimum factors (statutory) for public charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: IIRIRA codified minimum factors that must be considered in public charge determinations under INA section 212(a)(4): age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five factors are statutory (INA section 212(a)(4)(B), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4)(B)). DHS proposes to interpret these minimum statutory factors and to establish how officers should evaluate them under a clear framework; consideration is to be made in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age (IIRIRA factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Age is a required statutory factor to be considered when determining whether an alien is likely to become a public charge (IIRIRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the statutory minimum factors (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4)(B)); DHS will interpret and weigh age along with other factors in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health (IIRIRA factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Health is a required statutory factor to be considered when determining whether an alien is likely to become a public charge (IIRIRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes consideration of medical conditions and public health implications; DHS consulted HHS in prior guidance about how health indicators relate to public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status (IIRIRA factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Family status is a required statutory factor (IIRIRA) to be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will evaluate family size/composition and how family circumstances affect likelihood of reliance on public benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status (IIRIRA factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assets, resources, and financial status are required statutory factors (IIRIRA) for assessing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to assess income, assets, savings, and other financial indicators that bear on an alien's capacity for self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills (IIRIRA factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and skills are required statutory factors (IIRIRA) to be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes assessment of employment-related skills, educational attainment, and factors predictive of economic self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (consideration and required cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress generally permitted but did not require consular and immigration officers to consider an enforceable affidavit of support as a factor in inadmissibility determinations, except in certain cases where an affidavit of support is required and must be considered at least in that regard (INA section 212(a)(4)(B)(ii); INA section 213A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires affidavits of support for most family-based immigrants and certain employment-based immigrants and provides that these aliens are inadmissible unless a satisfactory affidavit of support is filed on their behalf (see INA section 213A, 8 U.S.C. 1183A). DHS will clarify the role of a sponsor's affidavit within public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS may consider receipt of public benefits even if eligible under PRWORA
rubrics_metrics.description: Although PRWORA made certain benefits available to some aliens, the receipt of such benefits was not exempted from consideration for purposes of INA section 212(a)(4); therefore, DHS may take into consideration receipt of public benefits for public charge determinations even if an alien may receive such benefits under PRWORA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble emphasizes no tension between availability of some benefits under PRWORA and Congress's intent to deny visas/admission/adjustment to aliens likely to become public charges; receipt of benefits may be relevant in future inadmissibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-cash, supplemental, and certain limited cash special purpose benefits historically not considered (INS 1999 position)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1999 proposed rule provided that non-cash, supplemental and certain limited cash, special purpose benefits should not be considered for public charge purposes in light of the INS definition by reference to primary dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INS's 1999 proposed rule and Interim Field Guidance expressed that such benefits (e.g., non-cash supplemental benefits) should not show primary dependence; DHS notes those interagency consultations and views were considered but states they may not remain fully relevant with the proposed change in standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond (mitigation for inadmissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alien is determined to be inadmissible on public charge grounds under INA section 212(a)(4), he or she may be admitted in the discretion of DHS, if otherwise admissible, upon the giving of a suitable and proper bond (INA section 213, 8 U.S.C. 1183).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble provides historical context: bond provisions date to the 19th/early 20th century and have been codified; Congress amended the section multiple times; regulations implementing the public charge bond are at 8 CFR 103.6 and 8 CFR 213.1. The bond may be returned except to the extent forfeited for violation of its terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability, exemptions, and tailored processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would apply to any alien subject to section 212(a)(4) who is applying for admission or adjustment of status before DHS; DOS screens applicants for visas. Processes, evidentiary requirements, and nature of stay differ across visa/admission/extension/change/adjustment contexts, and DHS proposes public charge processes appropriately tailored to the benefit sought (e.g., Form I-944 for adjustment of status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains applicants for admission (visa applicants, nonimmigrants) and applicants for adjustment of status undergo different processes and evidentiary standards; the proposed rule tailors requirements accordingly (see proposed 8 CFR 212.20 and other cited proposed sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of factual circumstances and totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes that certain factual circumstances would weigh heavily in favor of determining that an alien is not likely to become a public charge and other factual circumstances would weigh heavily in favor of determining that an alien is likely to become a public charge. Ultimately, each determination would be made in the totality of the circumstances based on consideration of the relevant factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of assigning greater weight to certain factual circumstances is to provide clarity for the public and immigration officers about how DHS would assess public charge admissibility; DHS cites proposed regulatory text (see proposed 8 CFR 212.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of aliens eligible for federal means-tested benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble lists categories of aliens eligible for federal means-tested benefits (in addition to qualified aliens after 5 years): refugees and asylees; aliens whose deportation was withheld under section 243(h) (8 U.S.C. 1253); Cuban and Haitian entrants; Amerasians; veterans lawfully residing (with honorable discharge meeting service requirement) and active duty personnel lawfully residing and their spouses/dependents; American Indian born in Canada or who is a member of an Indian tribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are specified in statute (8 U.S.C. 1613(b)(1) and related provisions) and identify populations eligible for certain federal means-tested benefits regardless of immigration status.

rubrics_metrics.name: State choice to follow federal 'qualified alien' definition and 'least restrictive means' presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA provided that a State that chooses to follow the Federal 'qualified alien' definition in determining aliens' eligibility for public assistance 'shall be considered to have chosen the least restrictive means available for achieving the compelling governmental interest of assuring that aliens be self-reliant in accordance with national immigration policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may enact their own legislation to provide public benefits to certain aliens not lawfully present; some States/localities have funded public benefits (especially medical and nutrition) that aliens may not be eligible for federally. Citation: 8 U.S.C. 1601(7) and 1621(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: HUD-administered housing/community development assistance (grandfathering clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs for housing or community development assistance or financial assistance administered by HUD, any program under title V of the Housing Act of 1949, or assistance under section 1926c of title 7 are exempt to the extent that the alien is receiving such a benefit on August 22, 1996.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow grandfathering exception tied to benefits already received on the specified date (see 8 U.S.C. 1611(b) clarifications in the preamble).
